It is true that the terms ‘human’ and ‘human being’ are not exactly the same. A body cell is human because it belongs to the species Homo sapiens; however, from fertilization onward, the embryo constitutes an organism of the human species, since it possesses its own biological organization and develops in an integrated manner according to its genetic program. Therefore, it is a human being.

The pro-life argument is not that anything biologically human has rights. A toe is human tissue and sperm is a human cell, but neither is a whole human organism. A fetus is not merely ‘human material’ it is a distinct developing human being. So your comparison confuses parts of a human with an actual human organism

You don’t have civil rights because you’re a human. You have rights because you’re a person. If your brain dies, you can still be alive, and you’re still a human, but you no longer have the qualities of being a person. For that reason, we allow brain dead people to be disconnected from life support without calling it murder. A fetus is not yet a person.

You are arguing semantics, while he is arguing biology. You misunderstand his claim. He very much claims that a fetus is a human BEING, because it is a distinct organism that is a member of the species homo Sapiens. This makes a fetus a human by being, not merely predication. A toe on the other hand is not distinct organism, rather a part of an organism, making it human by predication (adjective), but not by being (noun).

Jesus isn’t disappointed. The statement “humans deserve rights. Fetuses are human, therefore fetuses deserve rights” is not logically inconsistent, it’s just not complete. It’s ambiguous as to which of the 2 meanings for “human” we are predicating. If I say “Fetuses are human, therefore fetuses have rights” it would be entirely plausible for “human” to mean EITHER “a human being” OR “categorically human”. “Fetuses are human beings, therefore humans have rights” and “Fetuses are biologically part of the human species” are both completely plausible intended meanings from that statement, so it’s certainly ambiguous.

The pro-life advocates assertion is that the fetus is a human being that deserves rights. If the pro-life advocate seeks to prove their assertion (which this argument is part of), they can start by saying “Humans deserve rights. A fetus is human, therefore a fetus deserves rights.” If the first meaning is predicated, they are making an assertion “A fetus is a human being” that requires more proof. If they are predicating the second meaning, they are making a common-sense description of a human fetus that cannot be denied. Predicating this second meaning now requires the pro-life advocate to prove whether that life of the human variety is in fact a distinct human being. Either way, the argument is incomplete, but not logically dishonest.
